title: This Simple File Management System Changed My Life!
summary:
• Good file management balances form (how neatly things are organized) with function (naming files so you can search for them quickly).
• Folder structure: at most 5 folder levels deep and up to 99 numbered folders per level; the most-used folders get the lowest numbers and 99 is always the Archive.
• His top level: 01 Personal, 02 Work, 03 documents he references regularly, 04 Quick Share (a temporary folder for copies made just for sharing), a Backups folder, and 99 Archive.
• Naming: time-based files get a year, quarter, month or full date (a year or quarter is the most searchable). Everything else is sorted alphabetically with consistent keywords like doc, meeting notes, briefing, slides, form.
• Five tips: organize by where you will use something (David Allen); use your file app's built-in search and filters; add keywords to file descriptions; star 5 files at most; add shortcuts to shared files. Don't over-optimize: pick one system and stick to it.

title: Google’s NEW Prompting Guide is Incredible!
summary:
• According to Google's prompting guide, the most successful prompts average 21 words, while most people type fewer than nine.
• Tip 1, the power of three: ask for three variations in your first prompt (slogans, ad copy, email templates) to surface options you wouldn't have considered.
• Tip 2, multi-step workflows: break a big task into mini milestones, each with its own prompt, instead of one huge prompt (what he calls chain-of-thought prompting).
• Tip 3: ask the AI to brainstorm templates for your role, then have it draft the most useful one. Tip 4: do top-down research, moving from a broad overview to specific, actionable prompts.
• Tip 5 (Google users): open a PDF from Drive in Google Docs and use Gemini's 'Help me write' on it (needs the Google One AI Premium plan). In his test, Gemini summarized several URLs better than ChatGPT.

title: Stanford CS229 I Machine Learning I Building Large Language Models (LLMs)
summary:
• Training an LLM depends on five things: architecture, training loss/algorithm, data, evaluation, and systems. The lecturer skips architecture and argues that data, evaluation and systems matter most in practice.
• Pretraining is autoregressive next-token prediction with cross-entropy loss. Tokenizers (e.g. Byte Pair Encoding) matter a lot, and models are evaluated with perplexity and benchmarks like HELM, the Hugging Face Open LLM leaderboard, and MMLU.
• Data means crawling the web (Common Crawl, ~250 billion pages, ~1 PB), extracting text, filtering harmful content and PII, deduplicating, filtering by rules and by model, and reweighting domains. Top models train on ~15 trillion tokens.
• Scaling laws: more compute, data and parameters lower the loss predictably, so you tune small models and extrapolate. Chinchilla found ~20 tokens per parameter (~150 if you count inference cost), and his rough estimate puts Llama 3 405B at ~$75M to train.
• Post-training turns an LLM into an assistant: SFT (needs surprisingly little data), then RLHF with PPO or the simpler DPO, with LLMs increasingly replacing human labelers and judges (ChatBotArena, AlpacaEval, which prefer long answers). Systems tricks include mixed precision and operator fusion (torch.compile).

title: Master Data Analysis with ChatGPT (in just 12 minutes)
summary:
• The three-step DIG framework (Description, Introspection, Goal setting), which he learned in a Coursera AI-for-data-analysis course, turns ChatGPT into a personal data analyst with no technical skills needed.
• Description: upload the dataset, have ChatGPT list every column with a sample value, take 5 more random samples, then run a data quality check for missing values, odd formats and outliers.
• Introspection: ask for 10 interesting questions the data could answer, which columns each one needs and whether the data is sufficient, and which questions can't be answered because data is missing.
• He joins a second (made-up) dataset on a shared ID column (IMDb ID), which unlocks new analyses like cost per viewer by genre.
• Goal setting: state your goal and ask which parts of the data to focus on, which gives you a step-by-step roadmap. Pro tip: before presenting, ask what questions readers of your analysis will ask.
